docs.title: LQG: Inverse Optimal Control for Continuous Psychophysics
docs.text:
This repository contains the official JAX implementation of the inverse optimal control method presented in the paper:

Straub, D., & Rothkopf, C. A. (2022). Putting perception into action with inverse optimal control for continuous psychophysics. eLife, 11, e76635.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The package can be installed via pip:

python -m pip install lqg

Since publication of our eLife paper, I have substantially updated the package. If you want to use the package as described in the paper, please install an older version <0.2.0:

python -m pip install lqg==0.1.9

If you want the latest development version, I recommend cloning the repository and installing it locally with uv:

git clone https://github.com/RothkopfLab/lqg.git
cd lqg
uv sync

This creates a virtual environment in .venv with the package and all development dependencies (including those for tests and documentation). You can run commands in it with uv run, e.g. uv run pytest. If you want to contribute, run make install instead of uv sync, which also installs the pre-commit hooks.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation contains tutorials that illustrate how to use the lqg package to define optimal control models, simulate trajectories, and infer parameters from observed data:

  • Overview explains the model and its parameters, the extension to subjective internal models, and Bayesian inference of the parameters (based on my tutorial at CCN 2022).
  • Data fits models to data from a tracking experiment (Bonnen et al., 2015) with maximum likelihood estimation, compares them, and checks how well they reproduce the data.

Each tutorial is a Jupyter notebook, which you can find in docs/tutorials and run locally.

class System:
    def __init__(self, actor: LQGSpec, dynamics: LQGSpec):
        self.actor = actor
        self.dynamics = dynamics

    @property
    def T(self):
        """Length of trajectory

        Returns:
            int: number of time steps
        """
        return self.dynamics.A.shape[0]

    @property
    def xdim(self):
        """State dimensionality

        Returns:
            int: dimensionality of state
        """
        return self.dynamics.A.shape[1]

    @property
    def ydim(self):
        """Observation dimensionality

        Returns:
            int: dimensionality of observation
        """
        return self.dynamics.F.shape[1]

    @property
    def bdim(self):
        """Belief dimensionality

        Returns:
            int: dimensionality of belief
        """
        return self.actor.A.shape[1]

    @property
    def udim(self):
        """Action dimensionality

        Returns:
            int: dimensionality of action
        """
        return self.dynamics.B.shape[2]

    def simulate(
        self, rng_key, n=1, x0=None, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None, return_all=False
    ):
        """Simulate n trials

        Args:
            rng_key (jax.random.PRNGKey): random number generator key
            n (int): number of trials
            x0 (jnp.array): initial state
            xhat0 (jnp.array): initial belief
            Sigma0 (jnp.array): initial belief covariance
            return_all (bool): return estimates, controls and observations as well

        Returns:
            jnp.array: simulated states of shape (T, n, d)
        """

        Sigma0 = self.actor.V[0] @ self.actor.V[0].T if Sigma0 is None else Sigma0

        gains = lqr.backward(self.actor)
        K = kf.forward(self.actor, Sigma0=Sigma0)

        def simulate_trial(rng_key, x0=None, xhat0=None):
            """Simulate a single trial

            Args:
                rng_key (jax.random.PRNGKey): random number generator key
                T (int): number of time steps
                x0 (jnp.array): initial state
                xhat0 (jnp.array): initial belief

            Returns:
                jnp.array, jnp.array, jnp.array, jnp.array: x (states), x_hat (estimates), y, u
            """

            x0 = jnp.zeros(self.xdim) if x0 is None else x0
            xhat0 = jnp.zeros(self.bdim) if xhat0 is None else xhat0

            # generate standard normal noise terms
            rng_key, subkey = random.split(rng_key)
            epsilon = random.normal(subkey, shape=(self.T, self.xdim))
            rng_key, subkey = random.split(rng_key)
            eta = random.normal(subkey, shape=(self.T, self.ydim))

            def loop(carry, t):
                x, x_hat = carry

                # compute control based on agent's current belief
                u = gains.L[t] @ x_hat + gains.k[t]

                # apply dynamics
                x = (
                    self.dynamics.A[t] @ x
                    + self.dynamics.B[t] @ u
                    + self.dynamics.V[t] @ epsilon[t]
                )

                # generate observation
                y = self.dynamics.F[t] @ x + self.dynamics.W[t] @ eta[t]

                # update agent's belief
                x_pred = self.actor.A[t] @ x_hat + self.actor.B[t] @ u
                x_hat = x_pred + K[t] @ (y - self.actor.F[t] @ x_pred)

                return (x, x_hat), (x, x_hat, y, u)

            _, (x, x_hat, y, u) = scan(loop, (x0, xhat0), jnp.arange(self.T))

            return (jnp.vstack([x0, x]), jnp.vstack([xhat0, x_hat]), y, u)

        # simulate n trials
        x, x_hat, y, u = vmap(lambda key: simulate_trial(key, x0=x0, xhat0=xhat0))(
            random.split(rng_key, num=n)
        )

        if return_all:
            return x, x_hat, y, u
        else:
            return x

    def simulate_actions(
        self, x, action_dim_mask, rng_key, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None, return_all=False
    ):
        """Simulate cursor actions given pre-existing experimental target trajectories.

        Args:
            x (jnp.array): Experimental state data of shape (n, T+1, xdim)
            action_dim_mask (jnp.array): Boolean mask for cursor/action state dimensions
            rng_key (jax.random.PRNGKey): Random number generator key
            xhat0 (jnp.array, optional): Initial belief state
            return_all (bool): Whether to return intermediate estimates, controls, and obs

        Returns:
            jnp.array: Re-simulated state trajectories of shape (n, T+1, xdim)
        """
        Sigma0 = self.actor.V[0] @ self.actor.V[0].T if Sigma0 is None else Sigma0

        gains = lqr.backward(self.actor)
        K = kf.forward(self.actor, Sigma0=Sigma0)

        def simulate_trial_actions(x_single, action_dim_mask, rng_key, xhat0=None):
            # 1. Initial state at t=0 comes directly from experimental data x_single[0]
            x0 = x_single[0]
            xhat0 = jnp.zeros(self.bdim) if xhat0 is None else xhat0

            # Generate standard normal noise terms
            rng_key, subkey = random.split(rng_key)
            epsilon = random.normal(subkey, shape=(self.T, self.xdim))
            rng_key, subkey = random.split(rng_key)
            eta = random.normal(subkey, shape=(self.T, self.ydim))

            def loop(carry, t):
                x_curr, x_hat = carry  # x_curr is a 1D state vector of shape (xdim,)

                # Compute control based on agent's current belief
                u = gains.L[t] @ x_hat + gains.k[t]

                # Apply full dynamics transition: A[t] @ x_curr carries state & physics forward
                x_next_sim = (
                    self.dynamics.A[t] @ x_curr
                    + self.dynamics.B[t] @ u
                    + self.dynamics.V[t] @ epsilon[t]
                )

                # Splicing: Take fixed experimental target state for t+1,
                # but inject newly simulated cursor/action states
                x_next = (
                    x_single[t + 1].at[action_dim_mask].set(x_next_sim[action_dim_mask])
                )

                # Generate observation based on updated state x_next
                y = self.dynamics.F[t] @ x_next + self.dynamics.W[t] @ eta[t]

                # Update agent's belief
                x_pred = self.actor.A[t] @ x_hat + self.actor.B[t] @ u
                x_hat = x_pred + K[t] @ (y - self.actor.F[t] @ x_pred)

                return (x_next, x_hat), (x_next, x_hat, y, u)

            # Run scan across T time steps
            _, (x_steps, x_hat, y, u) = scan(loop, (x0, xhat0), jnp.arange(self.T))

            # Combine initial state x0 with simulated sequence -> shape (T+1, xdim)
            x_full = jnp.vstack([x0, x_steps])

            return x_full, jnp.vstack([xhat0, x_hat]), y, u

        # Map across trials and random keys
        keys = random.split(rng_key, num=x.shape[0])
        x_sim, x_hat, y, u = vmap(
            lambda x_i, key: simulate_trial_actions(
                x_i, action_dim_mask, key, xhat0=xhat0
            )
        )(x, keys)

        if return_all:
            return x_sim, x_hat, y, u
        else:
            return x_sim

    def conditional_moments(self, x, x0=None, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None):
        """Conditional distribution p(x | theta)

        Args:
            x: time series of shape T (time steps), n (trials), d (dimensionality)

        Returns:
            numpyro.distributions.MultivariateNormal: conditional distribution
        """
        T, obs_dim = x.shape
        xdim = self.dynamics.A.shape[1]
        bdim = self.actor.A.shape[1]

        # compute control and estimator gains
        gains = lqr.backward(self.actor)
        K = kf.forward(
            self.actor,
            Sigma0=self.actor.V[0] @ self.actor.V[0].T if Sigma0 is None else Sigma0,
        )

        # set up joint dynamical system for state and belief
        # p(x_t, xhat_t | x_{t-1}, xhat_{t-1})

        # joint dynamics
        F = jnp.concatenate(
            [
                jnp.concatenate([self.dynamics.A, self.dynamics.B @ gains.L], axis=-1),
                jnp.concatenate(
                    [
                        K @ self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.A,
                        self.actor.A
                        + self.actor.B @ gains.L
                        - K @ self.actor.F @ self.actor.A
                        + K
                        @ (
                            self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.B
                            - self.actor.F @ self.actor.B
                        )
                        @ gains.L,
                    ],
                    axis=-1,
                ),
            ],
            axis=-2,
        )

        # joint noise covariance Cholesky factor
        G = jnp.concatenate(
            [
                jnp.concatenate(
                    [
                        self.dynamics.V,
                        jnp.zeros(
                            (self.T, self.dynamics.A.shape[1], self.dynamics.W.shape[2])
                        ),
                    ],
                    axis=-1,
                ),
                jnp.concatenate(
                    [K @ self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.V, K @ self.dynamics.W],
                    axis=-1,
                ),
            ],
            axis=-2,
        )

        # initialize p(x_t, xhat_t | x_{1:t-1})
        if x0 is None:
            x0 = x[0]
        if xhat0 is None:
            xhat0 = x0
        mu0 = jnp.hstack(
            [x0, jnp.zeros(xdim - x0.shape[0]), xhat0, jnp.zeros(bdim - xhat0.shape[0])]
        )
        Sigma0 = G[0] @ G[0].T

        def scan_fn(carry, step):
            mu, Sigma = carry
            F, G, x = step

            # conditioning and marginalizing
            mu = F @ mu + (F @ Sigma)[:, :obs_dim] @ jnp.linalg.solve(
                Sigma[:obs_dim, :obs_dim], x - mu[:obs_dim]
            )

            Sigma = (
                F @ Sigma @ F.T
                + G @ G.T
                - (F @ Sigma)[:, :obs_dim]
                @ jnp.linalg.solve(
                    Sigma[:obs_dim, :obs_dim], (Sigma @ F.T)[:obs_dim, :]
                )
            )
            return (mu, Sigma), (mu, Sigma)

        _, (mu, Sigma) = scan(scan_fn, (mu0, Sigma0), (F, G, x[:-1]))
        # return jnp.vstack((mu0, mu)), jnp.vstack((Sigma0[jnp.newaxis], Sigma))
        return mu, Sigma

    def conditional_distribution(self, x, x0=None, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None):
        n, T, d = x.shape

        # compute p(x_{t+1}, xhat_{t+1} | x_{1:t})
        mu, Sigma = vmap(self.conditional_moments, in_axes=(0, 0, 0, None))(
            x, x0, xhat0, Sigma0
        )

        # marginalize out xhat by using only those entries of mu and Sigma that correspond to x
        return dist.MultivariateNormal(mu[:, :, :d], Sigma[:, :, :d, :d]).to_event(1)

    def log_likelihood(self, x, x0=None, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None):
        # log likelihood of the states at time t+1 given all previous states up to time t
        return self.conditional_distribution(
            x, x0=x0, xhat0=xhat0, Sigma0=Sigma0
        ).log_prob(x[:, 1:])

    def belief_tracking_distribution(self, x, Sigma0=None):
        d = self.xdim

        # compute p(x_{t+1}, xhat_{t+1} | x_{1:t})
        mu, Sigma = vmap(self.conditional_moments, in_axes=(0, None))(x, Sigma0)

        # return those elements of mu and Sigma that correspond to xhat
        return dist.MultivariateNormal(mu[:, :, d:], Sigma[:, :, d:, d:])

    def to_numpyro(self, Sigma0=None, xdim=None):
        return NumpyroLQG(self, Sigma0=Sigma0, xdim=xdim)

    def _repr_latex_(self) -> str:
        """
        Produces a Latex representation of the system.
        Can be used in jupyter notebooks via `display(system)`.

        Returns:
            str: Latex representation.
        """

        def bmatrix(arr: Array) -> str:
            """
            Produces a Latex bmatrix string representation of a given array.
            Adapted from https://stackoverflow.com/a/17131750.

            Args:
                arr (Array): Array to represent as bmatrix.

            Returns:
                str: Latex bmatrix representation.
            """
            assert jnp.ndim(arr) == 2

            lines = (
                jnp.array_str(arr, max_line_width=jnp.inf, precision=4)
                .replace("[", "")
                .replace("]", "")
                .splitlines()
            )

            rows = ["\\begin{bmatrix}"]
            rows += [" " + " & ".join(line.split()) + "\\\\" for line in lines]
            rows += ["\\end{bmatrix}"]
            bmatrix = "".join(rows)
            return bmatrix

        mats_dynamics = [
            self.dynamics.A,
            self.dynamics.B,
            self.dynamics.F,
            self.dynamics.V,
            self.dynamics.W,
            # self.dynamics.Q,
            # self.dynamics.R
        ]
        mats_actor = [
            self.actor.A,
            self.actor.B,
            self.actor.F,
            self.actor.V,
            self.actor.W,
            self.actor.Q,
            self.actor.R,
        ]
        mat_names = ["A", "B", "F", "V", "W", "Q", "R"]

        latex_str = "\\begin{align*} \\text{Dynamics:}"
        for mat, mat_name in zip(mats_dynamics, mat_names):
            latex_str += f" &&{mat_name} = {bmatrix(mat[0])}"

        latex_str += "\\\\"

        latex_str += "\\text{Actor:}"
        for mat, mat_name in zip(mats_actor, mat_names):
            latex_str += f" &&{mat_name} = {bmatrix(mat[0])}"

        latex_str += "\\end{align*}"
        return latex_str

def conditional_moments(self, x, x0=None, xhat0=None, Sigma0=None):
    """Conditional distribution p(x | theta)

    Args:
        x: time series of shape T (time steps), n (trials), d (dimensionality)

    Returns:
        numpyro.distributions.MultivariateNormal: conditional distribution
    """
    T, obs_dim = x.shape
    xdim = self.dynamics.A.shape[1]
    bdim = self.actor.A.shape[1]

    # compute control and estimator gains
    gains = lqr.backward(self.actor)
    K = kf.forward(
        self.actor,
        Sigma0=self.actor.V[0] @ self.actor.V[0].T if Sigma0 is None else Sigma0,
    )

    # set up joint dynamical system for state and belief
    # p(x_t, xhat_t | x_{t-1}, xhat_{t-1})

    # joint dynamics
    F = jnp.concatenate(
        [
            jnp.concatenate([self.dynamics.A, self.dynamics.B @ gains.L], axis=-1),
            jnp.concatenate(
                [
                    K @ self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.A,
                    self.actor.A
                    + self.actor.B @ gains.L
                    - K @ self.actor.F @ self.actor.A
                    + K
                    @ (
                        self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.B
                        - self.actor.F @ self.actor.B
                    )
                    @ gains.L,
                ],
                axis=-1,
            ),
        ],
        axis=-2,
    )

    # joint noise covariance Cholesky factor
    G = jnp.concatenate(
        [
            jnp.concatenate(
                [
                    self.dynamics.V,
                    jnp.zeros(
                        (self.T, self.dynamics.A.shape[1], self.dynamics.W.shape[2])
                    ),
                ],
                axis=-1,
            ),
            jnp.concatenate(
                [K @ self.dynamics.F @ self.dynamics.V, K @ self.dynamics.W],
                axis=-1,
            ),
        ],
        axis=-2,
    )

    # initialize p(x_t, xhat_t | x_{1:t-1})
    if x0 is None:
        x0 = x[0]
    if xhat0 is None:
        xhat0 = x0
    mu0 = jnp.hstack(
        [x0, jnp.zeros(xdim - x0.shape[0]), xhat0, jnp.zeros(bdim - xhat0.shape[0])]
    )
    Sigma0 = G[0] @ G[0].T

    def scan_fn(carry, step):
        mu, Sigma = carry
        F, G, x = step

        # conditioning and marginalizing
        mu = F @ mu + (F @ Sigma)[:, :obs_dim] @ jnp.linalg.solve(
            Sigma[:obs_dim, :obs_dim], x - mu[:obs_dim]
        )

        Sigma = (
            F @ Sigma @ F.T
            + G @ G.T
            - (F @ Sigma)[:, :obs_dim]
            @ jnp.linalg.solve(
                Sigma[:obs_dim, :obs_dim], (Sigma @ F.T)[:obs_dim, :]
            )
        )
        return (mu, Sigma), (mu, Sigma)

    _, (mu, Sigma) = scan(scan_fn, (mu0, Sigma0), (F, G, x[:-1]))
    # return jnp.vstack((mu0, mu)), jnp.vstack((Sigma0[jnp.newaxis], Sigma))
    return mu, Sigma

def max_likelihood(
    key,
    x,
    model=BoundedActor,
    numpyro_fn=lqg_model,
    max_steps=2_000,
    constraints=None,
    num_restarts=5,
    **fixed,
):
    """Maximum likelihood estimation of the parameters of an LQG model.

    The optimization is performed in an unconstrained space and mapped to the
    parameter space via the bijectors in ``constraints``. It is repeated from
    ``num_restarts`` random initializations, and the solution with the lowest
    negative log likelihood is returned.

    Args:
        key: jax.random.PRNGKey for sampling initial parameters
        x: observed data of shape (n_trials, T, d)
        model: model class (e.g. BoundedActor)
        numpyro_fn: numpyro model function defining the likelihood
        max_steps: maximum number of optimization steps per restart
        constraints: dict mapping parameter names to bijectors (e.g. Box, LogBox).
            Parameters not in this dict use the bounds in ``default_constraints``.
        num_restarts: number of random restarts of the optimization
        **fixed: parameters that are fixed to the given values (not estimated)

    Returns:
        dict: estimated parameters
    """
    constraints = {**default_constraints, **(constraints or {})}

    # bijectors are pytrees, so we close over them instead of passing them as args
    def loss(log_params, args):
        return _log_likelihood(log_params, args, constraints)

    def _fit(key):
        # sample initial parameters (in unconstrained space)
        initial_params = {
            name: random.normal(
                subkey,
                (),
            )
            for name, subkey in zip(
                get_model_params(model), random.split(key, len(get_model_params(model)))
            )
            if name not in fixed
        }
        solver = optx.LBFGS(rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)
        solution = optx.minimise(
            loss,
            solver,
            initial_params,
            args=(numpyro_fn, x, model, fixed),
            max_steps=max_steps,
            throw=False,
        )
        params = {
            name: constraints[name].forward(value)
            for name, value in solution.value.items()
        }
        return params, solution.state.f_info.f

    params, nll = jax.vmap(_fit)(random.split(key, num_restarts))
    params = {k: v[jnp.argmin(nll)] for k, v in params.items()}

    return params  # , losses

def parameter_recovery(
    key,
    model,
    num_datasets=100,
    T=500,
    num_trials=20,
    obs_dim=2,
    constraints=None,
    max_steps=1_000,
    num_restarts=10,
    progress=True,
    **fixed,
):
    """Parameter recovery analysis for a model class.

    For each of ``num_datasets`` repetitions, true parameters are sampled within the
    bounds of ``constraints`` (see ``sample_within_bounds``), data are simulated from
    the model, and the parameters are estimated with ``max_likelihood``.

    Args:
        key: jax.random.PRNGKey
        model: model class (e.g. BoundedActor)
        num_datasets: number of simulated data sets
        T: number of time steps per trial
        num_trials: number of trials per data set
        obs_dim: number of state dimensions used for fitting (as in experimental data,
            where only target and cursor position are observed)
        constraints: dict mapping parameter names to bijectors (e.g. Box, LogBox).
            Parameters not in this dict use the bounds in ``default_constraints``.
        max_steps: maximum number of optimization steps per restart
        num_restarts: number of random restarts of the optimization
        progress: show a progress bar
        **fixed: parameters that are fixed to the given values (not estimated)

    Returns:
        dict with entries
            "true" and "estimate": dicts mapping parameter names to arrays of shape (num_datasets,),
            "ll_true" and "ll_estimate": log likelihood of the data at the true and estimated
                parameters. An estimate that is far from the true value but has a higher
                likelihood points to a non-identifiable parameter, a lower likelihood
                to a failed optimization.
    """
    constraints = {**default_constraints, **(constraints or {})}
    free = [name for name in get_model_params(model) if name not in fixed]
    missing = [name for name in free if name not in constraints]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"No constraints for {missing}: pass them in `constraints` or fix them."
        )

    results = {
        "true": {name: [] for name in free},
        "estimate": {name: [] for name in free},
    }
    results["ll_true"], results["ll_estimate"] = [], []

    keys = random.split(key, num_datasets)
    if progress:
        from tqdm import tqdm

        keys = tqdm(keys)

    for dataset_key in keys:
        key_params, key_sim, key_fit = random.split(dataset_key, 3)

        true_params = {
            name: sample_within_bounds(subkey, name, constraints)
            for name, subkey in zip(free, random.split(key_params, len(free)))
        }
        x = model(**true_params, **fixed, T=T).simulate(rng_key=key_sim, n=num_trials)
        x = x[..., :obs_dim]

        estimates = max_likelihood(
            key=key_fit,
            x=x,
            model=model,
            constraints=constraints,
            max_steps=max_steps,
            num_restarts=num_restarts,
            **fixed,
        )

        for name in free:
            results["true"][name].append(true_params[name])
            results["estimate"][name].append(estimates[name])
        results["ll_true"].append(
            model(**true_params, **fixed, T=T).log_likelihood(x).sum()
        )
        results["ll_estimate"].append(
            model(**estimates, **fixed, T=T).log_likelihood(x).sum()
        )

    return {
        "true": {name: jnp.array(v) for name, v in results["true"].items()},
        "estimate": {name: jnp.array(v) for name, v in results["estimate"].items()},
        "ll_true": jnp.array(results["ll_true"]),
        "ll_estimate": jnp.array(results["ll_estimate"]),
    }

def plot_parameter_recovery(results, constraints=None):
    """Scatter plots of true vs. estimated parameters from ``parameter_recovery``.

    Parameters with a LogBox constraint are shown on a log scale.
    """
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    constraints = {**default_constraints, **(constraints or {})}
    names = list(results["true"])

    figure, axes = plt.subplots(
        1, len(names), figsize=(3 * len(names), 3), squeeze=False
    )
    for axis, name in zip(axes.flat, names):
        true, estimate = results["true"][name], results["estimate"][name]
        lims = [min(true.min(), estimate.min()), max(true.max(), estimate.max())]
        axis.scatter(true, estimate, alpha=0.7)
        axis.plot(lims, lims, "k--", alpha=0.5)
        axis.set_title(name)
        axis.set_xlabel("simulated value")
        if isinstance(constraints.get(name), LogBox):
            axis.set_xscale("log")
            axis.set_yscale("log")
    axes.flat[0].set_ylabel("estimated value")
    figure.tight_layout()
    return figure

def shared_params_lqg_model(
    x,
    model_type,
    process_noise=1.0,
    dt=1.0 / 60.0,
    priors=None,
    shared_params=None,
    dim=1,
    **fixed_params,
):
    """numpyro model for LQG models with shared parameter

    Args:
        x: data
        process_noise: target random walk standard deviation
        dt: time step duration
        priors: dict of prio distributions
        shared_params: list of parameter names that are shared across conditions
        dim: dimensionality of the state
        **fixed_params: any parameter that should be fixed (i.e. not estimated from the data)

    """
    # data shape is conditions, trials, time steps, state dimensionality
    Nc, N, T, d = x.shape

    # if not specifying extra priors, use the default ones from above
    if priors is None:
        priors = default_prior

    # which parameters will be shared across conditions?
    if shared_params is None:
        shared_params = []
    shared_params = set(shared_params)

    # get the parameter names of the current model type
    model_params = set(get_model_params(model_type).keys())

    # set up empty dict of parameters
    params = {}

    # these parameters will be shared across conditions
    for name in shared_params.intersection(model_params):
        # if a parameter is given in the fixed_params dict, we assume a fixed (user-specified) value
        if name in fixed_params:
            params[name] = fixed_params[name]
        # if not, we use one prior distribution across conditions
        else:
            params[name] = numpyro.sample(name, priors[name])

    # iterate over conditions
    for n in range(Nc):
        # get the data array for the current condition
        xn = x[n]

        # for those parameters that are not shared across conditions
        for name in model_params - shared_params:
            # define a prior distribution for that parameter in the current condition
            params[name] = numpyro.sample(f"{name}_{n}", priors[name])

        # set up the model, passing both shared and condition-specific parameters via the params dict
        lqg = model_type(process_noise=process_noise, dt=dt, T=T, dim=dim, **params)

        # likelihood
        numpyro.sample(f"x_{n}", lqg.conditional_distribution(xn), obs=xn[:, 1:])

def load_tracking_data(delay=12, clip=120, subtract_mean=True, data_path="data/"):
    """Load tracking data from Bonnen et al. (2015)

    Args:
        delay: temporal delay between target and response
        clip: clip the first n time steps
        subtract_mean: subtract the mean of both trajectories?

    Returns:
        np.array: data from tracking task
    """

    # factor to convert between pixels and acrmin
    arcscale = 1.32

    # load matlab file
    mat = loadmat(os.path.join(data_path, "data.mat"))

    # get target blob widths
    sigma = (mat["sigma"] * arcscale).round()
    sigmas = np.unique(sigma)

    # convert to numpy.float32
    target = mat["target"].astype(np.float32)
    mouse = mat["response"].astype(np.float32)

    # apply delay and clip the first couple of time steps
    if delay:
        target = target[:, clip:-delay]
        mouse = mouse[:, clip + delay :]
    else:
        target = target[:, clip:]
        mouse = mouse[:, clip:]

    # subtract the mean from both trajectories (in accordance with the analysis by Bonnen et al., 2015)
    # see https://github.com/kbonnen/BonnenEtAl2015_KalmanFilterCode/blob/master/tracking2graphs.m
    if subtract_mean:
        target = target - np.mean(target, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        mouse = mouse - np.mean(mouse, axis=1, keepdims=True)

    # stack data from all trials
    data = np.stack(
        [
            np.array(
                [
                    target[np.where(sigma == blob_width)[0], :],
                    mouse[np.where(sigma == blob_width)[0], :],
                ]
            )
            for blob_width in sigmas
        ]
    )

    # bring in right shape for our analysis methods
    data = data.transpose(0, 2, 3, 1)

    # subtract first time step in x dimension
    data = data - data[:, :, 0, 0][:, :, np.newaxis, np.newaxis]

    return data, sigmas

def minimize(
    fun,
    x0,
    method=None,
    args=(),
    bounds=None,
    constraints=(),
    tol=None,
    callback=None,
    options=None,
):
    """A simple wrapper for `scipy.optimize.minimize` using JAX.

    The objective is differentiated automatically with JAX, and parameters can
    be arbitrary PyTrees. The remaining keyword arguments are passed through to
    [`scipy.optimize.minimize`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.minimize.html);
    see its documentation for details.

    Args:
        fun (callable): The objective function to be minimized, written in JAX
            code so that it is automatically differentiable. Its signature is
            `fun(x, *args) -> float`, where `x` is a PyTree and `args` is a
            tuple of the fixed parameters needed to completely specify the
            function.
        x0: Initial guess represented as a JAX PyTree.
        method (str or callable, optional): Type of solver, e.g. `"BFGS"`,
            `"L-BFGS-B"` or `"SLSQP"`. If not given, chosen to be one of
            `BFGS`, `L-BFGS-B`, `SLSQP`, depending on whether the problem has
            constraints or bounds.
        args (tuple, optional): Extra arguments passed to the objective function
            and its derivative. Must consist of valid JAX types; e.g. the leaves
            of the PyTree must be floats.
        bounds (sequence or Bounds, optional): Bounds on variables for
            L-BFGS-B, TNC, SLSQP, Powell, and trust-constr methods. Bounds must
            be flattened manually in the same order as the inputs `x0`.
        constraints (Constraint, dict or list thereof, optional): Constraints
            definition (only for COBYLA, SLSQP and trust-constr). Constraints
            must be flattened manually in the same order as the inputs `x0`.
        tol (float, optional): Tolerance for termination.
        callback (callable, optional): Called after each iteration as
            `callback(xk)`, where `xk` is the current parameter vector
            represented as a PyTree.
        options (dict, optional): A dictionary of solver options, e.g.
            `maxiter` or `disp`.

    Returns:
        scipy.optimize.OptimizeResult: The optimization result. Its `x`
            attribute holds the solution, represented as a JAX PyTree.
    """
    # Use tree flatten and unflatten to convert params x0 from PyTrees to flat arrays
    x0_flat, unravel = ravel_pytree(x0)

    # Wrap the objective function to consume flat _original_
    # numpy arrays and produce scalar outputs.
    def fun_wrapper(x_flat, *args):
        x = unravel(x_flat)
        return float(fun(x, *args))

    # Wrap the gradient in a similar manner
    jac = jit(grad(fun))

    def jac_wrapper(x_flat, *args):
        x = unravel(x_flat)
        g_flat, _ = ravel_pytree(jac(x, *args))
        return onp.array(g_flat)

    # Wrap the callback to consume a pytree
    def callback_wrapper(x_flat, *args):
        if callback is not None:
            x = unravel(x_flat)
            return callback(x, *args)

    # Minimize with scipy
    results = scipy.optimize.minimize(
        fun_wrapper,
        x0_flat,
        args=args,
        method=method,
        jac=jac_wrapper,
        callback=callback_wrapper,
        bounds=bounds,
        constraints=constraints,
        tol=tol,
        options=options,
    )

    # pack the output back into a PyTree
    results["x"] = unravel(results["x"])
    return results

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we fit LQG models to data from a continuous tracking experiment using maximum likelihood estimation. The data come from Bonnen et al. (2015): Participants tracked a Gaussian blob following a random walk with the mouse cursor. The width of the blob was varied across six conditions, which makes the target position more or less uncertain.

We will

  1. load and visualize the data,
  2. fit two models from lqg.tracking (the BoundedActor and the SubjectiveActor) to each condition with lqg.infer.mle.max_likelihood,
  3. compare the models and check how well they reproduce the data.

Note: Fitting all models takes a few minutes on a laptop CPU.

docs.title: Loading the data¶
docs.text: load_tracking_data returns an array of shape (conditions, trials, time steps, 2), where the last dimension holds the target and the cursor position (in arcmin), and the blob widths of the six conditions.

docs.title: Maximum likelihood estimation¶
docs.text:
max_likelihood maximizes the log likelihood $\log p(\mathbf x_{1:T} \mid \theta)$ of a model class (see the Overview for how the likelihood is computed) with the L-BFGS optimizer from optimistix. Its main arguments are:

  • x: the data of one condition, with shape (trials, time steps, 2),
  • model: the model class whose parameters should be estimated,
  • constraints: lower and upper bounds for the parameters. The optimization runs in an unconstrained space, which is mapped to the bounds by a Box (linear scale) or a LogBox (log scale, useful for parameters that span several orders of magnitude). Parameters you do not specify use the bounds in lqg.infer.mle.default_constraints,
  • num_restarts: the number of random initializations. The optimizations run in parallel (via jax.vmap), and the solution with the highest likelihood is returned,
  • any further keyword argument (here: dt) fixes that parameter to the given value instead of estimating it.

docs.title: Bounded actor¶
docs.text: The BoundedActor has four free parameters: the perceptual uncertainty about the target (sigma_target) and about the cursor (sigma_cursor), the variability of the actions (action_variability) and the cost of actions (action_cost). We fit it separately to each condition.

docs.title: Subjective actor¶
docs.text:
The SubjectiveActor additionally assumes that the participant has a subjective internal model of the target's dynamics, in which the target also has a velocity component (see the Overview). This adds two parameters, subj_noise and subj_vel_noise.

When fitting this model with the default bounds, some estimates end up at the boundaries, for example action_cost at its upper bound of $10^{-2}$. We therefore widen the range of action_cost and let the two subjective noise parameters vary over four orders of magnitude on a log scale. Always check whether estimates lie at the boundaries. If they do, the bounds are probably too narrow.

docs.title: Model comparison¶
docs.text: The SubjectiveActor has two more parameters than the BoundedActor, so it is more flexible. To compare the models fairly, we penalize the number of parameters with the Akaike information criterion, $\text{AIC} = 2k - 2 \log \hat{L}$, where lower is better.

docs.title: Perceptual uncertainty¶
docs.text: The parameter of main interest is the perceptual uncertainty about the target. In both models, it increases with blob width, as expected.

docs.title: Simulating from the fitted models¶
docs.text: To see how well the fitted models capture the data, we simulate cursor responses to the same target trajectories that the participants saw, using simulate_actions, and compute the CCGs of the simulated data.

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text:
In the Hand dynamics tutorial, we extend both models with more realistic point-mass dynamics of the hand, which improves the fit to these data.

Maximum likelihood estimation gives point estimates. To quantify the uncertainty about the parameters, you can instead sample from their posterior distribution with MCMC, as shown in the Overview. lqg.infer.models also contains NumPyro models in which some parameters are shared across conditions (shared_params_lqg_model).

We can now simulate data from the model given the four parameters. To do this efficiently, we jit-compile the simulation function.

Some observations:

  • An increase in action costs leads to an increased lag and decreased maximum correlation.
  • An increase in perceptual uncertainty about the target leads to decreased correlation and increased lag, too, but the shape of the curves changes differently compared to the effect of the behavioral cost.
  • Action variability does not change the lag, but decreases correlation overall.
  • Perceptual uncertainty about the cursor does not change the shape of the CCGs at all, but does increase the mean squared error between target and response.

class SubjectiveActor(System):
    def __init__(self, 
               sigma_target, 
               action_variability, 
               action_cost, 
               sigma_cursor,
               sigma_s, 
               sigma_v):

        dt = 1. / 60.

        # true dynamical system (same as above)
        A = jnp.eye(2)
        B = jnp.array([[0.], [dt]])
        V = jnp.diag(jnp.array([1., action_variability]))

        C = jnp.eye(2)
        W = jnp.diag(jnp.array([sigma_target, sigma_cursor]))

        dynamics = Dynamics(A, B, C, V, W, T=T)

        # subjective dynamical system parameters
        A_subj = jnp.array([[1., 0., dt],  # target position
                            [0., 1., 0.],  # cursor position
                            [0., 0., 1.]]) # target velocity
        B_subj = jnp.array([[0.], [dt], [0.]])
        C_subj = jnp.array([[1., 0., 0.],
                            [0., 1., 0.]])
        V_subj = jnp.diag(jnp.array([sigma_s, action_variability, sigma_v]))

        # cost function
        Q = jnp.array([[1., -1., 0.],
                    [-1., 1., 0.],
                    [0., 0., 0.]])

        R = jnp.eye(1) * action_cost

        actor = Actor(A_subj, B_subj, C_subj, V_subj, W, Q, R, T=T)

        super().__init__(actor=actor, dynamics=dynamics)

docs.title: 1. NumPy-like API: jax.numpy¶
docs.text: JAX is a library that enables transformations of array-manipulating programs written with a NumPy-like API. You can think of JAX as differentiable NumPy that runs on accelerators. Many NumPy programs would run just as well in JAX if you substitute np for jnp.

docs.title: 2. Automatic differentiation: grad¶
docs.text:
You can think of jax.grad by analogy to the $ abla$ operator from vector calculus. Given a function $f(x)$, $ abla f$ represents the function that computes $f$’s gradient, i.e.

$$ ( abla f)(x)_i = rac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} (x). $$

Analogously, jax.grad(f) is the function that computes the gradient, so jax.grad(f)(x) is the gradient of f at x.

docs.title: 3. Easy vectorization: vmap¶
docs.text: In JAX, the jax.vmap transformation is designed to generate a vectorized implementation of a function automatically.

docs.title: 4. Compilation: jit¶
docs.text: You can use the XLA (accelerated linear algebra) compiler to compile your functions with jax.jit.

docs.title: Putting perception into action: Inverse optimal control for continuous psychophysics¶
Modeling a tracking task with LQG control¶
docs.text:
The LQG control problem is defined by a linear-Gaussian stochastic dynamical system $$ \mathbf x_{t+1} = A \mathbf x_t + B \mathbf u_t + V \mathbf \epsilon_t, \; \mathbf\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), $$

a linear-Gaussian observation model $$ \mathbf y_t = C \mathbf x_t + W \mathbf \eta_t, \; \mathbf\eta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), $$

and a quadratic cost function

$$ J = \sum_t \mathbf x_t^T Q \mathbf x_t + \mathbf u_t^T R \mathbf u_t. $$

We assume that the actor solves the linear-quadratic Gaussian problem, i.e. computes the Kalman filter $K$ and the LQR control law $L$, which are the optimal solution under the quadratic cost function

$$ J(u_{1:T}) = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf x_t^T Q \mathbf x_t + \mathbf u_t^T R \mathbf u_t. $$

We start by defining the matrices $A, B, C, V, W, Q, R$ as jax.numpy.arrays. according to our simple model of the continuous psychophysics tracking task:

$$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ dt \end{bmatrix}, \; C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \\ V = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_\text{rw} & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_\text{act} \end{bmatrix}, \; W = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma & 0 \\ 0 & \sigma_\text{cursor} \end{bmatrix}, \\ Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \; R = \begin{bmatrix} c \end{bmatrix}. $$

docs.title: Cross-correlograms¶
docs.text: We can also look at the correlation between the velocities of the target and the cursor at different time lags. This analysis is known as a cross-correlogram (Mulligan et al., 2013) and computes the average autocorrelation of the velocities of target and response.

docs.title: Influence of model parameters¶
docs.text: To look a the influence of the different model parameters, we define a class that inherits from the LQG base class and defines the matrices given the four parameters.

docs.title: Subjective internal models¶
docs.text:
The dynamical system that defines the experiment (i.e. the target movement) might not be known to the agent. In that case, we can assume that the agent has their own subjective internal model, which may differ from the true model.

For example, instead of the true random walk

$$ x_{t+1} = x_t + \sigma_\text{rw} * \epsilon_t,$$

the agent could assume that there is a velocity component to the random walk

$$ x_{t+1} = x_t + dt * v_t + \sigma_s * \epsilon_t \\ v_{t+1} = v_t + \sigma_v * \varepsilon_t. $$

Let's simulate this and compare it to the random walk on position that was used in the experiment.

docs.title: Likelihood function¶
docs.text:
To compute the likelihood

$$ p(\mathbf x_{1:T} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{T-1} p(\mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta), $$

we need to marginalize out the latent variables $\hat{\mathbf x}_{1:T}$ (the agent's internal beliefs). We can do this efficiently in the LQG setting by starting with our belief about the agent's belief $p(\hat{\mathbf x}_t \mid \mathbf x_{1:t})$ and then iteratively performing the following steps:

  1. Propagate the uncertainty about the agent's belief through the joint dynamical system of states and beliefs $$ p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}, \mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta) = \int p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}, \mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t}, \mathbf x_{t}, \theta) p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta) d \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t} $$
  2. Marginalize over the agent's belief $$ p(\mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta) = \int p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}, \mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta) d \hat{\mathbf x}_{t+1}$$
  3. Condition on the observed state $$ p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t+1}, \theta) = \frac{p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}, \mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta)}{p(\mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta)} $$

This gives us the contributions to the likelihood at each time step $p(\mathbf x_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t}, \theta)$ (2.) and the distribution over the agent's belief for the next time step $p(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf x_{1:t+1}, \theta)$ (3.).

This algorithm for computing the likelihood is implemented in the method log_likelihood(x) of our LQG class.

docs.title: Bayesian inference with NumPyro¶
docs.text:
In Bayesian inverse optimal control, we are interested in the posterior distribution of the model parameters given a trajectory

$$ p(\theta \mid \mathbf x_{1:T}) \propto p(\mathbf x_{1:T} \mid \theta) \, p(\theta). $$

To sample from this posterior distribution, we will use numpyro, a probabilistic programming package powered by jax. For every random variable in the model (in our case the parameters and the observed data), we need to call numpyro.sample to define a name and a distribution.

docs.title: Belief tracking¶
docs.text:
Once we have fit the model, we can use it to do belief tracking: We compute the probabilitiy distribution

$$ p(\hat{\mathbf x}_t | \mathbf x_{1:t}), $$

i.e. the researcher's uncertainty about the agent's belief.

def at_bounds(estimates, constraints, rtol=1e-3):
    # map -inf and +inf in unconstrained space to the lower and upper bounds
    flagged = []
    for condition, params in enumerate(estimates):
        for name, value in params.items():
            low = constraints[name].forward(-jnp.inf)
            high = constraints[name].forward(jnp.inf)
            # atol=0, otherwise every value below 1e-8 would count as close to the bound
            if jnp.isclose(value, low, rtol=rtol, atol=0) or jnp.isclose(value, high, rtol=rtol, atol=0):
                flagged.append((condition, name, float(value)))
    return flagged

Both extensions of the BoundedActor improve the fit in every condition, even after penalizing their additional parameters:

  • The point-mass hand dynamics improve the fit of both the bounded and the subjective model. The PointMassBoundedActor beats the BoundedActor in every condition, and the PointMassSubjectiveActor beats the SubjectiveActor in every condition.
  • The subjective internal model and the point-mass dynamics partly explain the same aspects of the data, so their improvements do not simply add up. Still, combining both helps: the PointMassSubjectiveActor has the lowest AIC in all conditions.

Which of the two extensions matters more depends on the condition: For small blob widths, the point-mass dynamics bring the larger improvement. For large blob widths, the subjective internal model does.

All models reproduce the qualitative pattern in the data: the CCG peaks get lower and broader with increasing blob width. The standard models produce peaks that are too low. The simulated peaks are still slightly earlier than in the data, so even the best model does not capture every aspect of the behavior.

docs.title: Hand dynamics¶
docs.text:
In the Data tutorial, we fitted the BoundedActor and the SubjectiveActor to the tracking data of Bonnen et al. (2015). In both models, the action directly sets the velocity of the cursor. Real hands cannot change their velocity instantaneously, though. In this tutorial, we fit two models with more realistic point-mass dynamics of the hand, the PointMassBoundedActor and the PointMassSubjectiveActor, and show that they explain the data better than their standard counterparts.

We follow the same steps as in the Data tutorial, so we explain only what is new here.

Note: Fitting all models takes about 15 minutes on a laptop CPU.

docs.title: Loading the data¶
docs.text: We load the data as in the Data tutorial and compute the cross-correlograms (CCGs) between target and cursor velocities, which we will compare with the models at the end.

docs.title: Standard models¶
docs.text: As a baseline, we fit the BoundedActor and the SubjectiveActor with the same settings as in the Data tutorial, which also explains the arguments of max_likelihood and the choice of bounds. We use the same number of restarts for all models in this tutorial.

docs.title: Point-mass hand dynamics¶
docs.text:
In the BoundedActor and the SubjectiveActor, the action directly sets the cursor velocity. The PointMassBoundedActor and the PointMassSubjectiveActor instead model the hand as a point mass driven by a muscle force with first-order dynamics (time constant tau), so the action changes the force, and the force accelerates the hand (see lqg.tracking.point_mass for the details). The state then contains the hand's velocity and force in addition to the target and cursor positions. Neither is observed in the data, but the likelihood takes care of this: it marginalizes over all state dimensions beyond the ones in x.

Apart from the dynamics, the two models are like their standard counterparts: The PointMassSubjectiveActor again has the two parameters subj_noise and subj_vel_noise of a subjective internal model of the target. The cost function now has extra terms for the hand's velocity (velocity_cost) and force (force_cost).

Two parameters need special treatment:

  • We fix the muscle time constant to tau = 0.066 s, a common value in the literature.
  • We fix force_cost = 0. When it is estimated, it goes to its lower bound in almost all conditions, however small that bound is, so it does not help to explain the data. It also makes the optimization much slower.

Because the action now is a change in force rather than a velocity, action_cost and action_variability are on a different scale than in the standard models. The estimates of action_cost are several orders of magnitude smaller, so we give it a wide range on a log scale.

Fitting the point-mass models is slower than fitting the standard models, because their state has more dimensions and they have more parameters.

docs.title: Model comparison¶
docs.text: The models differ in their number of parameters: The subjective models have two more parameters than their bounded counterparts, and the point-mass models have one more (velocity_cost) than the standard ones. To compare the models fairly, we penalize the number of parameters with the Akaike information criterion, $\text{AIC} = 2k - 2 \log \hat{L}$, where lower is better. We report the AIC of each model relative to the BoundedActor.

docs.title: Perceptual uncertainty¶
docs.text:
The parameter of main interest is the perceptual uncertainty about the target. It increases with blob width in all models, as expected. The only exception is the PointMassSubjectiveActor in the condition with the widest blob. The models agree on this trend but not on the absolute values: The point-mass models attribute more of the variability in the data to the motor system, so their estimates of sigma_target are smaller, at least for the smaller blob widths.

The exception at the widest blob suggests that sigma_target is not well constrained by these data in the PointMassSubjectiveActor: With more parameters, different combinations of them can explain the data almost equally well. A parameter recovery analysis (see below) can tell whether this is the case.

docs.title: Simulating from the fitted models¶
docs.text: To see how well the fitted models capture the data, we simulate cursor responses to the same target trajectories that the participants saw, using simulate_actions, and compute the CCGs of the simulated data. For the point-mass models, we pad the data with zeros for the hand velocity and force, which are simulated by the model, too.

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text: The point-mass models have more parameters, and some of them (for example tau) we fixed to values from the literature. To check whether the remaining parameters can be identified from data like these, run a parameter recovery analysis: simulate data from the model with known parameters, fit the model to the simulated data, and compare the estimates with the true values. lqg.infer.mle.parameter_recovery does this for any model class, and python -m lqg.infer.mle runs it from the command line.
